title: Introducing sociology
subject: Sociology
summary: Sociology studies human society, social relationships and the patterns behind everyday life.
points: Sociology emerged in Europe with industrialisation and new questions about social order.
It studies both small interactions and large structures such as class and state.
The sociological imagination connects personal troubles with public issues.
It differs from common sense by using systematic evidence and theory.
example: Unemployment is a personal problem for one worker but a structural issue when a whole industry declines.
mistakes: Treating sociology as opinion or common sense.
Ignoring the link between individual and structure.

title: Terms, concepts and their use in sociology
subject: Sociology
summary: Sociology uses concepts such as society, community, association, institution, status, role and social group.
points: Society is a web of relationships; a community is based on shared locality or identity.
An association is deliberately formed for a purpose; an institution is an established pattern of norms.
Status is a position in society; role is the expected behaviour attached to it.
Groups may be primary (close, personal) or secondary (formal, impersonal).
Ascribed status is inherited; achieved status is earned.
example: A family is a primary group and an institution; a bank is a secondary group and an association.
aliases: terms concepts and their use in sociology

title: Understanding social institutions
subject: Sociology
summary: Family, marriage, kinship, religion, education, economy and polity are institutions that organise social life.
points: Family types include nuclear and extended, patrilineal and matrilineal.
Marriage rules include endogamy (within a group) and exogamy (outside a group).
Kinship links people through blood and marriage.
Religion provides meaning, ritual and social cohesion but can also divide.
Institutions change with economy, law and culture.
example: A matrilineal system traces descent and inheritance through the mother's line.
mistakes: Assuming the nuclear family is universal.

title: Culture and socialisation
subject: Sociology
summary: Culture is learned and shared, and socialisation transmits it from one generation to the next.
points: Culture includes norms, values, beliefs, language and material objects.
Ethnocentrism judges other cultures by one's own; cultural relativism avoids that.
Socialisation happens through family, school, peers and media.
Agents of socialisation may conflict, producing different values.
Sanskritisation and Westernisation are examples of cultural change in India.
example: A child learning table manners at home is being socialised into cultural norms.
mistakes: Judging another culture by your own standards.

title: Doing sociology: research methods
subject: Sociology
summary: Sociologists use surveys, interviews, observation, case studies and documents to study society.
points: Quantitative methods count and compare; qualitative methods interpret meaning.
A sample must represent the population for findings to generalise.
Participant observation studies people in their own setting.
Ethics require consent, confidentiality and avoiding harm.
Triangulation combines methods to strengthen conclusions.
example: A researcher living in a village to study migration is doing participant observation.
mistakes: Assuming a small convenient sample represents everyone.

title: The demographic structure of Indian society
subject: Sociology
summary: India's population structure — age, sex, rural-urban split and migration — shapes its society.
points: India's demographic transition has lowered death rates before birth rates.
A young population creates a demographic dividend if educated and employed.
Sex ratio imbalances reflect social preferences and discrimination.
Migration is rural-to-urban, seasonal and increasingly circular.
Ageing, urbanisation and employment are key policy concerns.
example: A falling sex ratio at birth signals son preference rather than a natural imbalance.
mistakes: Reading sex ratio as a biological fact.

title: Social institutions: continuity and change
subject: Sociology
summary: Caste, tribe, family and marriage in India have changed while retaining continuities.
points: Caste has been transformed by law, education and politics but persists in marriage and networks.
Tribal societies are diverse and not isolated from the wider economy.
Family forms are shifting towards nuclear households in cities.
Marriage practices such as dowry persist despite legal prohibition.
State law and social movements have driven reform.
example: Caste-based matrimonial advertisements show how caste continues in private choice.

title: Patterns of social inequality and exclusion
subject: Sociology
summary: Inequality is structured along caste, class, gender and minority status and produces exclusion.
points: Caste inequality involves graded hierarchy and untouchability.
Class inequality comes from unequal access to income, education and property.
Gender inequality appears in wages, property, mobility and unpaid work.
Minorities face exclusion in access to services and representation.
Affirmative action and social movements respond to exclusion.
example: Manual scavenging is an extreme form of caste-based occupational exclusion.
aliases: patterns of social inequality and exclusion

title: The challenges of cultural diversity
subject: Sociology
summary: India's diversity of language, religion and region raises questions of unity, federalism and minority rights.
points: Regionalism may be a positive identity or a demand for autonomy.
Federalism accommodates diversity through shared and separate powers.
Minority rights protect language, culture and religion.
Communalism treats religion as the basis of political community and is a major challenge.
Secularism and constitutional patriotism offer integrative frameworks.
example: Linguistic states accommodated language diversity without breaking the union.

title: Structural change
subject: Sociology
summary: Colonialism, industrialisation and urbanisation reshaped India's social structure.
points: Colonial rule integrated India into a global economy and created new administration and classes.
Industrialisation created factories, new occupations and urban migration.
Urbanisation changed family, neighbourhood and work life.
New classes include industrialists, professionals and the working class.
Structural change is uneven across regions and sectors.
example: Mill towns such as Bombay grew as workers migrated from rural districts.
mistakes: Ignoring colonial roots of modern institutions.

title: Cultural change
subject: Sociology
summary: Social reform, modernisation, secularisation and new media have changed Indian culture.
points: Nineteenth-century reform movements challenged sati, caste and gender norms.
Modernisation involves new technology, education and rational outlooks.
Secularisation means the declining hold of religion over public institutions, not necessarily belief.
Sanskritisation is upward mobility by adopting higher-caste practices.
Cultural change can be resisted and uneven.
example: The spread of English education created new professional groups and aspirations.

title: Change and development in rural society
subject: Sociology
summary: Land reform, the Green Revolution and migration have changed rural society and agriculture.
points: Land reforms abolished intermediaries in some states but implementation varied.
The Green Revolution raised output while increasing regional inequality.
Agricultural labourers and marginal farmers remain vulnerable.
Migration and remittances sustain many rural households.
Rural society is stratified by land, caste and gender.
example: Punjab and Haryana benefited most from Green Revolution technology.
aliases: change and development in rural society

title: Change and development in industrial society
subject: Sociology
summary: Industrialisation created new work relations, trade unions and informal labour.
points: Factories separated ownership from work and created wage labour.
Trade unions organised workers for wages and conditions.
The informal sector employs most workers without security.
Global production chains and subcontracting changed factory work.
Technology alters skills and employment patterns.
example: Home-based garment workers are part of formal supply chains but lack formal protection.
mistakes: Equating industrial work with formal employment.

title: Globalisation and social change
subject: Sociology
summary: Globalisation increased flows of goods, capital, people and culture, with uneven social effects.
points: Liberalisation in 1991 opened India to foreign investment and trade.
Globalisation created new jobs in services and IT while displacing some traditional work.
Cultural flows spread ideas but also provoke resistance.
Inequality widened between regions and skill groups.
Global institutions influence national policy.
example: Business process outsourcing created urban service jobs tied to global clients.
mistakes: Assuming its benefits are evenly shared.

title: Mass media and communications
subject: Sociology
summary: Mass media shape public opinion, culture and politics, and their ownership matters.
points: Media include print, broadcast and digital platforms.
Media can inform and mobilise but also spread stereotypes and misinformation.
Ownership concentration and advertising influence content.
Digital media changed participation and surveillance.
Media literacy helps evaluate claims.
example: A viral rumour can trigger violence before it is verified.

title: Social movements
subject: Sociology
summary: Social movements organise collective action for change or resistance around shared grievances.
points: Movements may be reformist, revolutionary, or resistance movements.
They use protest, mobilisation, litigation and media.
Identity movements form around caste, gender, environment or region.
Movements can institutionalise into parties or NGOs.
Repression, co-option and internal division affect outcomes.
example: The Chipko movement mobilised villagers to protect forests.

title: What is psychology?
subject: Psychology
summary: Psychology studies behaviour and mental processes, using scientific methods rather than intuition.
points: It examines experience and behaviour in context.
Branches include cognitive, developmental, social, clinical and organisational psychology.
Themes include nature versus nurture and stability versus change.
Psychology is applied in education, health, work and sport.
Popular psychology differs from evidence-based psychology.
example: A clinical psychologist uses assessment and therapy, not guesswork, to understand distress.

title: Methods of enquiry in psychology
subject: Psychology
summary: Psychologists use observation, experiments, surveys, tests and case studies with ethical safeguards.
points: Experiments manipulate an independent variable to study its effect on a dependent variable.
Correlation shows association, not causation.
Interviews and questionnaires collect self-reports but may be biased.
Reliability means consistency; validity means measuring what is intended.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality and no harm.
example: A study linking sleep hours and test scores finds correlation, not proof that sleep causes scores.

title: Human development
subject: Psychology
summary: Development across the lifespan involves physical, cognitive, social and emotional changes.
points: Development is lifelong, multidimensional and influenced by heredity and environment.
Piaget described stages of cognitive development from sensorimotor to formal operations.
Erikson described psychosocial stages across the lifespan.
Attachment in infancy shapes later relationships.
Adolescence involves identity formation and peer influence.
example: Object permanence develops in infancy, when a child knows an object exists even when hidden.
mistakes: Treating development as only physical growth.
Assuming all children reach stages at the same age.

title: Sensory, attentional and perceptual processes
subject: Psychology
summary: Sensation detects stimuli, attention selects them, and perception organises them into meaningful experience.
points: Absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus detected; difference threshold is the smallest detectable change.
Attention is selective and limited in capacity.
Perception uses Gestalt principles such as proximity, similarity and closure.
Depth perception uses binocular and monocular cues.
Illusions show that perception is constructed, not copied.
example: A mirage in a desert is a perceptual illusion, not a real pool of water.
mistakes: Treating perception as a direct copy of reality.

title: Learning
subject: Psychology
summary: Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour or knowledge resulting from experience.
points: Classical conditioning pairs a neutral stimulus with one that already produces a response.
Operant conditioning shapes behaviour through reinforcement and punishment.
Observational learning occurs by watching models.
Reinforcement schedules affect how persistent a learned behaviour is.
Cognitive learning includes insight and latent learning.
example: A dog salivating at the sound of a bell is classical conditioning.
mistakes: Assuming learning is always visible immediately.

title: Human memory
subject: Psychology
summary: Memory encodes, stores and retrieves information through sensory, short-term and long-term systems.
points: Sensory memory lasts a fraction of a second; short-term memory holds a few items briefly.
Long-term memory has large capacity and includes explicit and implicit memory.
Chunking and rehearsal improve short-term retention.
Forgetting results from decay, interference and retrieval failure.
Serial position effects show better recall of first and last items.
example: Remembering a phone number by grouping digits uses chunking.
mistakes: Thinking memory works like a recording.

title: Thinking
subject: Psychology
summary: Thinking involves mental representation, problem solving, reasoning and decision making.
points: Problem solving uses algorithms, heuristics and insight.
Heuristics are fast but can produce biases.
Reasoning may be deductive (from general to specific) or inductive.
Creativity involves divergent thinking and flexibility.
Language and thought influence each other.
example: Assuming a cheap product is poor quality is a heuristic that may mislead.

title: Motivation and emotion
subject: Psychology
summary: Motivation drives goal-directed behaviour, and emotion involves physiological, cognitive and expressive components.
points: Motives may be biological (hunger, sleep) or psychosocial (achievement, affiliation).
Maslow arranged needs from physiological to self-actualisation.
Intrinsic motivation comes from interest; extrinsic from rewards.
Basic emotions include happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust.
Stress affects motivation and health.
example: Studying because the subject interests you is intrinsic motivation.
mistakes: Ignoring the cognitive appraisal of emotion.

title: Variations in psychological attributes
subject: Psychology
summary: People differ in intelligence, aptitude, creativity and personality, measured with psychological tests.
points: Intelligence includes reasoning, problem solving and adaptation.
Spearman proposed a general factor; Gardner proposed multiple intelligences.
IQ scores are standardised with a mean of 100.
Aptitude predicts potential in a domain; achievement measures what has been learned.
Tests must be reliable and valid, and used ethically.
example: A child of 10 with a mental age of 12 has an IQ of 120 on the ratio formula.
mistakes: Treating IQ as a complete measure of ability.

title: Self and personality
subject: Psychology
summary: Self-concept is how we understand ourselves, and personality is a stable pattern of behaviour and traits.
points: Self includes personal identity and social identity.
Freud described id, ego and superego with psychosexual stages.
Trait theories describe personality in dimensions such as the Big Five.
Assessment methods include self-report inventories and projective tests.
Personality is shaped by heredity, environment and culture.
example: A person high in conscientiousness tends to be organised and dependable.
mistakes: Treating personality types as fixed boxes.
Assuming a single test captures personality fully.

title: Meeting life challenges
subject: Psychology
summary: Stress arises when demands exceed resources, and coping and resilience determine its effects.
points: Stressors may be physical, social or psychological.
The general adaptation syndrome describes alarm, resistance and exhaustion stages.
Coping may be problem-focused or emotion-focused.
Social support and appraisal shape stress responses.
Relaxation, exercise and time management help manage stress.
example: Reframing an exam as a challenge rather than a threat changes the stress response.

title: Psychological disorders
subject: Psychology
summary: Psychological disorders are patterns of distress or impairment classified in diagnostic systems.
points: Disorders include anxiety, mood, psychotic, eating and substance-related conditions.
Classification aids communication but carries stigma risk.
Symptoms must be judged against cultural norms and duration.
Biological, psychological and social factors interact.
Early recognition improves outcomes.
example: Persistent low mood and loss of interest for weeks may indicate a depressive disorder.
mistakes: Labelling everyday sadness as a disorder.
Assuming one cause explains a disorder.

title: Therapeutic approaches
subject: Psychology
summary: Therapy treats psychological distress through psychological, biological and social approaches.
points: Psychodynamic therapy explores unconscious conflict.
Behaviour therapy uses conditioning to change behaviour.
Cognitive therapy changes distorted thinking patterns.
Humanistic therapy emphasises self-acceptance and growth.
Biomedical treatment uses medication under medical supervision.
example: Gradual exposure in behaviour therapy reduces a phobia by controlled steps.
mistakes: Assuming one therapy suits every problem.

title: Attitude and social cognition
subject: Psychology
summary: Attitudes are evaluations of objects and people, and social cognition explains how we interpret social information.
points: Attitudes have cognitive, affective and behavioural components.
Prejudice is an attitude; discrimination is behaviour.
Attribution explains behaviour by internal dispositions or external situations.
Stereotypes simplify social perception and can distort it.
Persuasion depends on source credibility, message and audience.
example: Blaming a person's failure on laziness while ignoring circumstances is a attribution error.

title: Social influence and group processes
subject: Psychology
summary: Groups shape behaviour through conformity, obedience, norms and collective decision making.
points: Conformity is pressure to match group norms.
Obedience to authority can override personal judgement.
Group polarisation pushes decisions towards extremes.
Groupthink reduces critical evaluation.
Cooperation and competition both shape group performance.
example: A committee that suppresses dissent may reach a worse decision through groupthink.
mistakes: Assuming groups always decide better than individuals.

title: Psychology and life
subject: Psychology
summary: Psychology applies to health, environment, work and community life.
points: Health psychology studies stress, illness and health behaviour.
Environmental psychology studies how settings affect behaviour.
Work psychology covers motivation, leadership and job design.
Community psychology addresses wellbeing in social context.
Applications must respect culture and ethics.
example: A hospital designs waiting areas to reduce anxiety, using environmental psychology.
mistakes: Assuming findings transfer across cultures unchanged.

title: Developing psychological skills
subject: Psychology
summary: Psychological skills include observation, listening, interviewing, empathy and ethical practice.
points: Effective helpers listen actively and reflect feelings.
Observation must be systematic and free of premature inference.
Interviewing uses open questions and avoids leading the respondent.
Empathy means understanding another's frame of reference.
Ethics include confidentiality, boundaries and referral.
example: Reflecting back 'you sound overwhelmed' helps a client feel heard.
mistakes: Giving advice before understanding the problem.

title: Practical work in geography: maps and scales
subject: Geography
summary: Practical geography covers map scales, projections, representation of data, surveying and GIS.
points: A map scale relates distance on the map to distance on the ground.
Large-scale maps show small areas in detail; small-scale maps show large areas.
Map projections flatten the curved earth and distort shape, area or distance.
Data can be shown by choropleth, isopleth, dot and flow maps.
Surveying and GIS measure and analyse spatial data.
example: On a 1:50,000 map, 2 cm represents 1 km on the ground.
mistakes: Assuming a projection preserves all properties at once.
